# Kosala Saṁyutta (SN 3)

**ID:** SN 3
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kosala Saṁyutta* (SN 3) is a major collection within the *Saṁyuttanikāya* centered on encounters between the Buddha and King Pasenadi of Kosala [Galasek 2016]. Pasenadi appears as a primary interlocutor at the opening of every discourse, depicted across a wide range of conversations as a devoted lay disciple whose relationship with the Buddha began early in the teacher's career [Galasek 2016]. The discourses characteristically set verses within substantive prose narratives that present the king as a complex, relatable figure navigating the moral struggles and temptations of sovereignty, including warfare, judicial governance, espionage, and personal grief [Anālayo 2016].

Individual suttas address diverse practical and spiritual questions. In SN 3.8, Queen Mallikā engages Pasenadi on the theme of the self as dearmost, presenting a narrative and conceptual parallel to the dialogue between Yājñavalkya and Maitreyī in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* [Kuznetsova et al. 2012]. In SN 3.13 (*Doṇapākasutta*), the Buddha advises Pasenadi on mindful eating and thorough chewing to counter overeating and maintain health [Anālayo 2018]. In SN 3.16, the Buddha comforts the king upon the birth of a daughter, affirming the spiritual and moral capacity of women [Collett 2014]. In SN 3.22 (*Ayyikāsutta*), the Buddha consoles Pasenadi following the death of his grandmother, illustrating universal mortality with the simile of a potter's clay vessels that all ultimately break [Anālayo 2016]. The collection and its Chinese parallels have served as a basis for comparative textual studies by Mun-keat Choong [Meisig 2010].

 DharmaNexus confirms these relationships with high-scoring cross-language alignments to T 99, T 100, T 125, T 127, the Sanskrit *Udānavarga*, *Cīvaravastu*, and *Saṅghabhedavastu*, as well as Tibetan Vinaya commentaries [DharmaNexus]. Internally, DharmaNexus detects extensive text reuse across the Pali canon, sharing substantial passages with the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (AN 4, AN 3, AN 6, AN 10), the *Magga Saṁyutta* (SN 45), the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2), and the *Sattajaṭila Sutta* (Ud 6.2) [DharmaNexus].
